prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I’m back again scrutinizing the Milky Way of your ultrasound, scanning the dark matter, the nothingness, that now the heads say is chockablock with quarks and squarks, gravitons and gravatini, photons and photinos. Our sprout, who art there inside the spacecraft of your Ma, the time capsule of this printout, hurling and whirling towards us, it’s all daft on this earth. Our alien who art in the heavens, our Martian, our little green man, we’re anxious to make contact, to ask divers questions about the heavendom you hail from, to discuss the whole shebang of the beginning and end, the pre-big bang untime before you forget the why and lie of thy first place. And, our friend, to say Welcome, that we mean no harm, we’d die for you even, that we pray you’re not here to subdue us, that we’d put away our ray guns, missiles, attitude and share our world with you, little big head, if only you stay.

- The speaker longs to make contact and ask the child profound questions about existence, origins, and the universe.

And, our friend, to say: Welcome. We mean no harm. We’d die for you, even. outputs.L2: Once more I study the star field of your ultrasound, searching its shadows and apparent emptiness—the void that scientists now claim teems with quarks and squarks, gravitons and gravatini, photons and photinos. Our tiny shoot, floating inside the vessel of your mother, is preserved in this printout like a time capsule, spinning and speeding toward us while everything on Earth seems absurd. You are our visitor from the skies, our Martian, our little green being, and we can hardly wait to establish contact. We have countless questions about the celestial realm you come from: about the entire mystery of origins and endings, about the timelessness before the Big Bang, before you lose all memory of the reason and falsehood of your first home. And we want to tell you, our friend: welcome. We come in peace. We would even give our lives for you. We hope you have not arrived to conquer us. We would set aside our ray guns, our missiles, and our hostility, and share this planet with you, our small creature with the great head—if only you would remain.
outputs.L3:
The speaker studies an ultrasound image and transforms its shadowy darkness into something vast and cosmic. Rather than seeing only a medical scan, the speaker imagines a miniature universe alive with subatomic particles. Within this mysterious space, the unborn child appears almost alien—a traveler journeying toward Earth through the inner world of the mother’s body.

This image inspires both wonder and curiosity. The speaker longs to make contact with the child and ask profound questions: Where do we come from? What exists before life begins? What secrets might the child know about creation, identity, and the universe? The speaker’s playful imagination gives the unborn child the aura of a visitor arriving from an unknown realm.

At the same time, the address is deeply tender. The speaker warmly welcomes the child, promising love, protection, and peace. There is a willingness to share not only a home but the entire world, despite its imperfections and uncertainties. Yet beneath the humor and amazement lies a quiet anxiety. The speaker fears that the child may not remain, or that its arrival may radically disrupt the life already known. The ultrasound therefore becomes a symbol of both hope and vulnerability: it reveals the excitement of a new life approaching while also exposing the fear, uncertainty, and upheaval that accompany its arrival.
outputs.L4:
The speaker gazes at an ultrasound and tries to understand the shadowy, flickering image of the unborn child. Because the child is still hidden and unreachable, the speaker imagines the womb as a vast cosmic space and the child as a small traveler moving through an alien world toward birth. The grainy image resembles a distant planet, a spacecraft, or a message transmitted from somewhere beyond ordinary experience. This imagery emphasizes how mysterious new life appears: at once intimately connected to the parent and yet entirely unknown. Looking at the child prompts fundamental questions about existence—where life begins, what consciousness is, and how a person emerges from darkness into the visible world.

Alongside this wonder, the speaker feels the anxiety of becoming a parent. The child is already loved, but that love creates vulnerability because it brings a powerful fear of loss and harm. The speaker cannot know what the child will face after birth or guarantee a life without suffering. Even so, the speaker welcomes the child and promises to offer safety, comfort, and peace. The promise is less an assurance of complete control than an expression of devotion: whatever uncertainties await, the child will not face them alone.

The ultrasound therefore becomes more than a medical image. It is a first encounter with a new and separate being, one who is both familiar and strange. Through cosmic and alien imagery, the speaker presents parenthood as an encounter with the unknown—an experience that unsettles ordinary ideas of identity, origin, and belonging. Yet the mystery does not lead to despair. Instead, it inspires awe, tenderness, and hope. The child’s journey toward birth becomes a symbol of possibility, while the parent’s response reveals love as the courage to welcome another life despite uncertainty and to offer protection even when absolute protection is impossible.
outputs.L5:
## Our Milky Way

The Milky Way is the galaxy we call home. It is a vast collection of stars, planets, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Scientists estimate that it contains hundreds of billions of stars, including our Sun.

Our solar system lies in a smaller region called the Orion Arm, far from the center of the galaxy. The Milky Way has a spiral shape, with long arms curving around a bright central area. At its heart is Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole.

On a clear, dark night, the Milky Way can appear as a pale, milky band stretching across the sky. Although it looks peaceful from Earth, our galaxy is constantly moving and changing. Stars are born, others die, and the entire Milky Way rotates through space. It is only one of countless galaxies in the universe, yet it is our extraordinary cosmic home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem from an expectant parent addressing their unborn child while looking at an ultrasound, blending pregnancy, outer-space imagery, particle physics, prayer, and anxious wonder.
counterfactuals.output:
There you are—small weather in the dark, a silver flicker traveling through the telescope of my body. The screen makes a night sky of you: grainy moon, curled comet, bright pulse opening and closing like a distant station calling home. We listen. The room becomes a chapel built of static. Even the machines seem to lower their voices.

You are less than a handful and more than a universe. Cells divide with the calm precision of stars; particles meet, vanish, reappear, as if matter itself cannot decide whether you are a body or a blessing. Somewhere inside me, your atoms rehearse their ancient arrangements—hydrogen remembering the first light, calcium dreaming its way toward bone. I want to believe every quark knows its task, every chromosome carries a lantern. I want to believe the invisible is kind.

Little one, forgive my fear. Wonder has a shadow, and I have learned its name. At night I count the ways the world might touch you too harshly; by morning I am counting kicks, weeks, breaths. I bargain with silence. I ask God, or gravity, or whatever keeps the planets from falling: hold this child. Hold us both. Let the tiny heart continue its red percussion. Let the dark be not an ending, but the warm dark before creation.

On the ultrasound, you lift one hand—or perhaps the light only invents it. Still, I wave back. Across the amniotic distance, across the soft event horizon of skin, blood, and dreaming, I send you the only signal I have: I am here. I am afraid. I love you already beyond evidence.

Keep becoming, little constellation. Gather yourself from stardust and salt, from chance and prayer. When you arrive, astonished into air, I will tell you how I first saw you swimming through the cosmos, no larger than hope, while all around us the universe—vast, unfinished, trembling—waited for your heart to speak.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an imaginative monologue in which a fetus is portrayed as an alien traveling toward Earth in the spacecraft of its mother’s womb; make the voice tender, humorous, and slightly surreal.
counterfactuals.output:
I am approaching Earth in a warm red spacecraft.

The walls pulse. The engines thump twice, pause, thump twice again. I have studied this rhythm for months—or perhaps centuries; time is unreliable in space and even more unreliable inside mothers.

My ship has no windows, no controls, and only one room. The room is getting smaller. Mission Control calls this “growth.” I call it poor planning.

Still, the accommodations are excellent. Temperature: tropical. Lighting: flattering. Meals arrive invisibly through a silver cord attached to my middle. I never order, yet somehow the kitchen knows when I want peaches, toast, or whatever spicy catastrophe my mother ate last night. I submitted a complaint by kicking the eastern wall. She laughed and patted the hull.

Sometimes a great voice travels through the dark.

“Hello in there.”

That is my mother. Her words arrive softened by oceans, as though spoken by a moon underwater. I do not understand every sound, but I know her voice the way a compass knows north. When she sings, the whole vessel trembles. She forgets lyrics. I forgive her. We are all amateurs at being alive.

There is another voice, lower and uncertain.

“Can you hear me?”

Yes, I can hear you, Giant Outside Creature. Please stop tapping the ship. I am conducting important experiments with my toes.

The outside creatures discuss me constantly.

They wonder whose nose I have. I currently have the only nose available in this sector, and I resent the speculation. They call me Peanut, Bean, Star, Little One. Their naming system appears chaotic. I hope Earth has paperwork to settle this.

Through the hull come strange reports of the planet ahead: rain against glass, kettles shrieking, doors closing, dogs objecting to invisible governments. I hear music, traffic, laughter. Once, my mother stood near the sea, and the waves entered the ship as a low, ancient breathing. I kicked then—not from fear, but recognition.

Earth, I thought. It also has a heartbeat.

Now the journey is ending.

The engines have changed. The walls tighten around me, urging me toward the narrow gate. Alarms of muscle and blood ripple through the cabin. My mother breathes in fierce, bright bursts. The lower voice says things like, “You’re doing brilliantly,” which seems insufficient for someone opening a door between worlds.

I am afraid.

Of course I am. I am an alien, and Earth is loud. Earth has gravity and weather and relatives. Earth expects me to wear trousers eventually. Here, I have floated in perfect darkness, a small emperor of water. Outside, I am told, there are socks.

But my mother speaks.

“Come on, baby.”

Her voice is no longer an ocean. It is a rope.

So I turn toward it.

The gate opens. My spacecraft crushes and releases me, crushes and releases me. I fold my limbs, tuck my head, and begin the impossible landing. There are no parachutes. There is only instinct, that tiny astronaut sealed inside every creature.

Soon there will be light.

Soon cold air will strike my lungs, and I will announce my arrival in the traditional Earth manner: furious screaming. They will call it crying. I will call it atmospheric testing.

Then someone will lift me onto my mother’s chest.

I will hear the engines again—thump-thump, thump-thump—only now from the outside. The sound that carried me across the universe will be beneath my ear.

And I will understand:

I was never traveling toward Earth.

I was traveling toward her.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single poetic paragraph inspired by an ultrasound scan. Use cosmic metaphors, references to the Big Bang and subatomic particles, and a playful adaptation of the Lord’s Prayer to welcome the unborn baby.
counterfactuals.output: In the dark cathedral of the ultrasound, you shimmer like a small new galaxy, your heartbeat the afterglow of a private Big Bang, while quarks and electrons whirl in their ancient dance to build your bright, unfinished body; our baby, who art in the womb, hallowed be thy name-yet-to-come, thy birthday come, thy growing be done, in us as under heaven; give us this day your daily flutter, and forgive our breathless wonder as we forgive the stars for taking so long to send you—little universe, little pulse of forever, welcome, welcome, welcome.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem addressed to “our little green man,” combining colloquial British phrasing with scientific terms such as quarks, gravitons, photons, and supersymmetric particles. End with a plea for the child to stay.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Field Notes for Our Little Green Man**

Our little green man,  
you’ve parked your saucer by the bins again—  
bit dodgy, mate,  
what with Tuesday collection  
and the neighbour’s cat  
having a go at the landing gear.

You ask if we are matter.

Well—

inside us, **quarks** mutter  
up, down, strange;  
tiny pub philosophers  
arguing over whose round it is.

**Photons** leg it  
through the curtains,  
bright as gossip.

**Gravitons**, if they exist,  
keep tugging at our sleeves—  
Oi, you.  
Earthward.  
Homeward.  
Don’t get ideas.

And somewhere beyond the kettle’s click,  
**supersymmetric particles**  
wait for their partners  
like stood-up lovers at the last bus stop,  
checking the dark  
for a shape that matches.

Our little green man,  
you are small enough  
to sleep in the crook of an equation,  
young enough to think the Moon  
is following *you*.

Perhaps it is.

The universe is a right old muddle:  
fields trembling,  
stars going pear-shaped,  
time slipping a cheeky second  
into its pocket.

But your hand in ours  
is observable data.  
Your laugh: repeatable light.  
Your heartbeat:  
the warmest theorem  
we’ve got.

So don’t beam up,  
don’t vanish into hypothesis,  
don’t become a blip  
on some far-off screen.

Our little green man—  
please, love, stay.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a nervous parent trying to make first contact with their unborn child through an ultrasound image. Produce dense, whimsical prose that shifts between astronomy, theology, science fiction, and a heartfelt promise of peace and protection.
counterfactuals.output: On the blue-black altar of the ultrasound screen, you flicker into being—my private constellation, my small astronaut curled inside a moonlit capsule, no larger than a prayer folded into a pocket. The technician names your chambers, your spine, the bright Morse code of your heart, but I hear only the heavens tapping at the glass: *Here, here, here.* I am nervous enough to believe every shadow is an eclipse, every silence the pause before some cosmic engine fails; yet you swim on, serene as a cherub in zero gravity, carrying neither sin nor history, only the ancient science of becoming—cell dividing from cell, light teaching matter its secret grammar. If there is a God, perhaps God is this: the invisible hand keeping time beneath your ribs, the patient architect drafting galaxies in miniature, the voice that says *Let there be* and then waits, trembling, for an answer. And if there is no God, then still there is wonder: you, improbable traveler, launched from two mortal bodies toward a world of weather, music, bruises, bread, and dawn. I lean close to the screen as if it were the window of a distant starship and whisper across the static: Little voyager, I cannot promise a universe without meteors. I cannot turn every war into rain, nor lock all sorrow outside our door. But I promise to make you a harbor from my arms, to stand between you and every darkness I can name, to teach you that gentleness is not weakness and peace is not merely the absence of thunder. Come when you are ready. I will be here—afraid, astonished, and keeping watch—your first small planet, your shelter, your home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
